We have been exploring vectors and vector operations in three-dimensional space, and we have developed equations to  describe lines, planes, and spheres. In this section, we use our knowledge of planes and spheres, which are examples of  three-dimensional figures called surfaces, to explore a variety of other surfaces that can be graphed in a three- dimensional coordinate system.  Identifying Cylinders  The first surface we’ll examine is the cylinder. Although most people immediately think of a hollow pipe or a soda straw  when they hear the word cylinder, here we use the broad mathematical meaning of the term. As we have seen,  cylindrical surfaces don’t have to be circular. A rectangular heating duct is a cylinder, as is a rolled-up yoga mat, the cross- section of which is a spiral shape. Quadric Surfaces  We have learned about surfaces in three dimensions described by first-order equations; these are planes. Some other  common types of surfaces can be described by second-order equations. We can view these surfaces as three- dimensional extensions of the conic sections we discussed earlier: the ellipse, the parabola, and the hyperbola. We call  these graphs quadric surfaces.
